Prologue

All writers work to authorize their writings as best they can: some with trustworthy witnesses; others with other writers who have written before them, whose testimonies are accepted as certain; others with the testimony of Holy Scripture. All these foundations have been lacking for me, to authorize what I have written in these twelve books; and I find no other foundation to authorize it, except to set down here an account of the diligence I exercised to learn the truth of everything I have written in these books. As I have said in another prologue of this work: I was commanded, by holy obedience from my superior, to write in the Mexican language what I thought would be useful for the doctrine, culture, and maintenance of Christianity among the natives of this New Spain, and to aid the workers and ministers who instruct them. Having received this command, I made a draft or memorandum of all the subjects in Castilian that were to be treated — which is what is written in the twelve books, the postilla, and the songs — and this was first set down in the town of Tepepulco, which is in the province of Aculhuacan Otescucui, and it was done in this manner. In the said town I had all the leading men assembled, together with the lord of the town, who was called don Diego de Mendoza, an elderly man of great standing and ability, very experienced in all matters of government, war, politics, and even idolatry. Having assembled them, I explained to them what I intended to do, and asked them to provide me with capable and experienced persons with whom I could converse and who could give me an account of what I asked them. They answered that they would speak among themselves about the matter and would give me an answer the next day; and so they took their leave of me. The next day the lord came with the leading men, and after a very solemn speech, as they were accustomed to make, they pointed out to me ten or twelve elderly leading men, and told me that with those I could confer, and that they would give me an account of everything I asked them. Also present there were up to four scholars whom I had some years before taught grammar at the college of Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco. With these leading men and also the scholarly leading men I conversed for many days, for nearly two years, following the outline of the draft I had made. All the matters we discussed were given to me in the form of pictures, for that was the writing they had anciently used, and the scholars declared them in my language, writing the explanation at the foot of the picture. I still have these originals now. Also during this time I composed the postilla and the songs, which these same men wrote down in the same town of Tepepulco. When Father Fray Francisco Toral, who had imposed this task upon me, went to the chapter where his term was fulfilled, I was moved from Tepepulco, taking all my writings, and went to lodge at Santiago de Tlatelolco, where I assembled the leading men and explained to them the matter of my writings, and asked them to appoint some capable leading men with whom I could examine and discuss the writings I had brought written from Tepepulco. The governor with the aldermen pointed out to me about eight or ten leading men, chosen from among all, very skilled in their language and in matters of their antiquities; and with four or five students, all trilingual, shut away for about a year in the college, everything I had brought written from Tepepulco was corrected, clarified, and added to; and everything was written out again in a neat hand, because it had been written in great haste. The one who worked hardest of all the students in this review or examination was Martín Jacobita, who was then rector of the college, a resident of Tlatelolco from the neighborhood of Saint Anne. Having done the above at Tlatelolco, I came to reside at Saint Francis of Mexico with all my writings, where over a period of three years I went through all my writings alone again and again, corrected them again, divided them into books, into twelve books, and each book into chapters, and the books into chapters and paragraphs. After this, while Father Fray Miguel Navarro was provincial and Father Fray Diego de Mendoza was guardian of the convent of Mexico, with their support all twelve books were copied out fair in a good hand, and the postilla and the songs were corrected and copied fair, and an art of the Mexican language was made with a vocabulary of [words]; and the Mexicans corrected and added many things to the twelve books as the fair copy was being made. So that the first copy by which my works were composed...

fo.2.

The first group was from Tepepulco; the second, from Tlatelolco; the third, from Mexico: and in all these examinations there were grammar school students. The principal and most learned was Antonio Valencia, a resident of Azcapotzalco; another, slightly less so, was Alonso Vegerano, a resident of Cuauhnáhuac; another was Martín Jacobita, whom I mentioned above; another, Pedro de San Buenaventura, a resident of Cuauhnáhuac: all of them expert in three languages — Latin, Spanish, and Indigenous. The scribes who copied all the works in good handwriting are: Diego de Grado, resident of Tlatelolco, from the neighborhood of La Concepción; Bonifacio Maximiliano, resident of Tlatelolco, from the neighborhood of San Martín; Mateo Severino, resident of Xochimilco, from the district of Villac. Once these writings had been drafted in clean copy, with the help of the fathers named above — on which many coins were spent on the scribes — the author of them requested of the father commissary, Fray Francisco de Ribera, that they be reviewed by three or four friars, so that those men could give their opinion of them at the provincial chapter, which was approaching. These men reviewed them and gave their report at the provincial definitorio at that same chapter, saying what they thought of them, and they said in the definitorio that they were writings of great value and that they ought to be favored so that they could be completed. Some of the definitors felt it was contrary to poverty to spend money on writing out those texts; and so they ordered the author to dismiss the scribes and to write by himself alone whatever he wished in them. He, being more than seventy years old and suffering from a trembling hand, could write nothing, nor could a dispensation from this order be obtained: and so the writings remained, with nothing done in them, for more than five years. During this time, at the following chapter, Fray Miguel Navarro was elected custos of the custody for the general chapter, and Fray Alonso Escalona as provincial. At this time, the author made a summary of all the books, and of all the chapters of each book, and of the prologues, in which, briefly, was said all that was contained in the books. This summary was taken to Spain by Father Fray Miguel Navarro and his companion, Father Fray Jerónimo de Mendieta; and so it became known in Spain what had been written concerning the things of this land. In the meantime, the father provincial took all the books from the said author, and they were scattered throughout the whole province, where they were seen by many friars and approved as very precious and beneficial. After some years, Father Fray Miguel Navarro, returning from the general chapter — having come as commissary for these parts — recovered the said books under censure, with notice to the author; and once they were gathered, about a year more or less passed before they came back into the author's possession. During this time nothing was done with them, nor was there anyone to support finishing the translation into Spanish — until Father Commissary General Fray Rodrigo de Sequera came to these parts, saw them, was very pleased with them, and ordered the said author to translate them into Spanish; and he provided everything necessary so that they could be written out anew, with the Mexican language in one column and the Spanish in the other, in order to send them to Spain — because the Most Illustrious Lord Don Juan de Ovando, President of the Council of the Indies, had sought them, having learned of these books through the summary that the said Father Fray Miguel Navarro had taken to Spain, as was said above. All of the foregoing is relevant so that it may be understood that this work has been examined and refined by many people over many years, and that many hardships and misfortunes have been endured in order to bring it to the state in which it now stands.

End of the Prologue.

To the sincere reader.

It is worth noting, for the understanding of the calendar that follows: that the months are unequal to ours, in number and in days, because the months of these native peoples number eighteen, and each one of them has no more than twenty days, and thus all the days contained in these months total three hundred and sixty. The last five days of the year do not fall within any month, but rather are left outside the count, as idle days. The months of these native peoples are marked at the beginning of the calendar by their count and by letters of the alphabet; on the other side, our months are marked by letters of the alphabet and by their count. And thus one can easily understand on which day of our months each of their feasts falls. The moveable feasts, which are compiled at the end of the calendar, follow a different system of counting, which they used in the divinatory art, and which contains two hundred and sixty days; in this count there are feasts, and because this count does not follow the count of the year, nor does it have as many days, the feasts end up varying, falling on different days from one year to the next.

fo. 3

Book Two, which treats of the feasts and sacrifices with which these natives honored their gods in the time of their infidelity.

Chapter One, of the calendar of fixed feasts, the first of which is what follows.

The first month of the year was called among the Mexicans Atlcaoalo, and in other places Quavitlcoa. This month began on the second day of the month of February, when we celebrate the Purification of Our Lady. On the first day of this month they celebrated a feast in honor (according to some) of the gods called Tlalocs, whom they held to be gods of rain; and according to others, in honor of their sister, the goddess of water, Chalchiuhtlicue; and according to still others, in honor of the great priest or god of the winds, Quetzalcoatl; and we may say it was in honor of all of these. This month, like all the others — eighteen in total — has twenty days each.

Book Two

The second month was called Tlacaxipeoaliztli. On the first day of this month, they held a festival in honor of the god called Totec, who was also known by another name, Xipe, during which they killed and flayed many slaves and captives.

Chapter 2.

10. KL. Tlacaxipeoalistli. 22. Cathedra of Saint Peter.

2. To the captives they were going to kill: they pulled out the hair from their crowns, and their own masters kept it like relics. They did this in the neighborhood temple before the fire.

4. When the lords brought their captives' slaves to the temple where they were to be killed, they led them by the hair. And as they climbed the steps of the temple, some of the captives fainted, and their owners dragged them up by the hair to the place

6. where they were to die.

7. Arriving at the sacrificial stone — which was a stone about three palms high, or a little more, and two palms wide — they threw them on it face up. Five men held them: two by the legs, two by the arms, and one by the head. Then the priest who was to kill them came forward and struck them in the chest with both hands using a flint stone shaped like an iron lancet, and through the hole it made he inserted his hand and tore out the heart, which was then offered to the sun and placed in a gourd bowl.

10-13. After removing the heart and pouring the blood into a gourd bowl — which was received by the lord whose captive it had been — they rolled the body down the temple steps, where it came to rest on a small plaza below. From there, certain old men called quaquacuiltin took it back and carried it to the neighborhood temple, where they cut it up and divided it among themselves to eat.

16. Before cutting up the captives, they flayed them, and others dressed themselves in their skins. Then they engaged in mock combat with other young men, as if in war, capturing one another.

18. After what was described above, they killed other captives by fighting with them. These captives were tied by the middle of their body with a rope that passed through the hole of a millstone, long enough for the captive to walk around the full circumference of the stone. They were given weapons with which to defend themselves, and then four warriors came against them with swords and shields, fighting them one by one until they defeated them.

On the Fixed Feasts. Folio 4

The third month was called Tocoztonli. On the first day of this month, they held a feast for the god called Tlaloc, who is the god of rains. During this feast, they killed many children on the mountains and offered them in sacrifice to this god and his companions, so that he would give them water.

Chapter 3.

KL Tocoztonli.

During this feast, they offered the first fruits of the flowers that had grown for the first time that year, at the temple called Topico. Before offering them, no one dared to smell a flower.

The officials of the flowers, who were called sochimanque, held a feast for their goddess called Coatlyeue, and by another name Coatlatona.

Also during this month, those who had been wearing the skins of the dead — who had been flayed the previous month — undressed themselves, and went to throw them into a cave at the temple called Topico. They went to do this in a procession, with many ceremonies, and they went stinking like dead dogs. After they had left them there, they bathed themselves with many ceremonies. Some sick people made a vow to be present at this procession in order to be healed of their illnesses, and it is said that some were indeed healed.

The owners of the captives, along with all those of their household, did penance for twenty days, during which they neither bathed nor washed their heads, until the skins of the dead captives were placed in the cave mentioned above. They said they did penance on account of their captives.

After they had finished the penance, they bathed and washed themselves, and invited all their relatives and friends, and gave them food, and performed many ceremonies with the bones of the dead captives.

Throughout these twenty days, until the arrival of the next month, they practiced singing in the houses called cujicoali — not dancing, but seated — singing songs in praise of their gods. Many other things were done during this feast, which are described at length in its history, folio 45, 27.

The fourth month was called Huey Tozoztli. On the first day of this month they held a festival in honor of the god called Cinteotl, who was considered the god of maize. In his honor, they fasted for four days before the festival arrived.

Chapter 4.
1 Huey Tozoztli.

2 In this festival, they placed cattail reeds at the doors of their houses and adorned them with blood from their ears or from their shins. The nobles and the wealthy, in addition to the cattail reeds, decorated their houses with branches called acxoatl. They also decorated
3-4 their gods with these, and placed flowers before whichever gods each person kept in his house.
5-6 After this, they went through the cornfields and gathered ears of maize that were still small, adorned them with flowers, and brought them to place before their gods, at the house called calpulli. They also placed food before them.
7-11 After doing this in the neighborhoods, they went to the temple of the goddess called Chicomecóatl. There, before her, they staged mock combats in the manner of battles. All the young women carried on their backs ears of maize from the previous year and went in procession to present them to the goddess Cihuacoatl. They then brought them back home as blessed objects, and from that maize they took the seed for planting the coming year. They also applied it to their faces with the roots, as a blessing from her.
12-15 They made an image of this goddess from dough called tzoalli, in the courtyard of her temple. Before it they offered all kinds of maize, all kinds of beans, and all kinds of chia seeds, because they said she was the originator and giver of those things, which are the foods that sustain life.
16-20 According to the account of some: the children who were to be sacrificed were gathered in the first month, paired with their mothers, and went along in all the festivals thereafter, until the rains began to come. Thus they sacrificed some in the first month called Quiahuitl, others in the second called Tlacaxipehualiztli, others in the third called Tozoztontli, and others in the fourth called Huey Tozoztli. In this way, until the rains came abundantly, children were sacrificed at every festival. Many other ceremonies were performed at this festival.

The fifth month was called Toxcatl. On the first day of this month they held a great feast in honor of the god called Titlacaoa, and by another name Tezcatlipuca. This god they held to be the god of gods. In his honor they killed at this feast a chosen young man who had no blemish on his body, raised in all pleasures for the space of one year, instructed in playing music, singing, and speaking.

Book Two.

The sixth month was called Etzalqualiztli. On the first day of this month they held a festival for the rain gods. In honor of these gods, the priests of these gods fasted for four days before the festival arrived, which were the four last days of the previous month.

Chapter 6.

KL Etzalqualiztli.

For the celebration of this festival, the temple priests and their ministers went to gather rushes at Citlaltepec, which grow very large and very beautiful in a body of water called Temilco. From there they brought them to Mexico to adorn the temples. Along the road where they traveled, no one appeared — all travelers hid themselves out of fear of them. And if they came across anyone, they would strip that person of everything down to bare skin, and if the person defended himself, they would beat him so badly as to leave him for dead. And even if he was a tribute-collector for Moctezuma, they would seize his goods — yet no punishment was given to them for this, because as ministers of the idols they had the freedom to do these things, and others also without any penalty. Many other ceremonies were performed by the temple priests during these four days, which are set out at length in the history of this festival.

When the feast of Etzalqualiztli arrived, everyone made a kind of porridge or gruel called Etzalli, a food dedicated to the occasion. Everyone ate it in their homes, and gave it to those who came by, and they engaged in all manner of revelry on that day.

During this same festival, those ministers of the idols who had been negligent in their service were terribly punished in the waters of the lake, so severely that they were left for dead. They were left there at the water's edge, where their parents or relatives would come to take them and carry them home half dead.

In this same month they also killed many captives and slaves, adorned with the regalia of the gods called Tlalocs. In honor of these gods, they killed them at this same temple, and the hearts of those who were killed were thrown into the whirlpool at the drainage of the Lake of Mexico, which could be clearly seen on [certain days]. Many other ceremonies were performed.

Concerning the fixed feasts, folio 6.

The seventh month was called Tecuilhuitontli. On the first day of this month they held a feast for the goddess of salt, whom they called Huixtocihuatl. They said she was the elder sister of the rain gods, the Tlalocs. In honor of this goddess they killed a woman dressed in the same ornaments with which the goddess herself was depicted.

Chapter 7.

KL. Tecuilhuitontli.    f  2. [Feast of] Marcellinus, Peter, and others.

On the vigil of this feast all the women — old women, young women, and girls — sang and danced, holding on to short cords that they carried in their hands, each gripping one end and the next gripping the other. These cords were called Sochimecatl. They all wore garlands of the flowers of the plant called Utoueilatl, which certain old men had prepared; these old men danced at the sides of the procession. In the midst of the women walked she who was the image and likeness of this goddess and who was to die, adorned with rich ornaments.

On the night before the feast the women kept vigil with the one who was to die, and they sang and danced all night long. When morning came, they all dressed themselves, and the priests performed a very solemn areito (ceremonial song and dance). All those who were present at the areito held in their hands those flowers called cempoalxochitl. Dancing in this manner, they led many captives to the temple of Tlaloc, and with them the woman who was to die — who was the image of the goddess Huixtocihuatl. There they first killed the captives and afterward killed her.

Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, and also much drunkenness. All of this is set forth at length in the history of this feast, folio 76.

Second Book

The eighth month was called Veitzcuylhuitl. On the first day of this month, a feast was held for the goddess called Xilonen, goddess of the tender green ears of maize. In this feast, food was given to all the poor — men and women, old men and old women, boys and girls — in honor of this goddess. They killed a woman ten days into this month, dressed in the same ornaments worn by the goddess herself.

Chapter 8.

KL Veitzeuylhuitl — 22 — Saints' day of Paul

1. They gave food to thin and large men and women for eight continuous days before the feast.
2. Then very early in the morning they gave them a drink of a kind of porridge they call chiempinol,

6. they scolded him and took away what he had, and he went away with nothing. The lords did this to console the poor, because at this time of year food is ordinarily scarce.

7. All these eight days they danced and performed; holding a ritual dance — men and women all together,
8. all very finely adorned with rich garments and jewels. The women let their hair loose and
9. went about with their hair down, dancing and singing with the men. This ceremony began at sunset and they continued it until
10. nine o'clock at night. They carried small torches and large hat-shaped pine-wood brands, and there were many braziers or
11. bonfires burning in the same courtyard where they danced. In this dance or ceremony they went
12. clasping each other's hands or embracing, with one person's arm wrapped around another's body in an embrace, and
13. likewise the other — both men and women. The day before they were to kill the woman who was to die in honor of the goddess Xilonen,
14. the women who served in the temple (called tioalimactas, who performed ritual dances in the courtyard of that same temple) chanted the praises and songs
15. of this goddess, and all went surrounding the woman who was to die, who went arrayed in the ornaments of this goddess. Singing in this manner,
16. they proceeded along; they kept vigil all the night before the day on which she was to die.
17. At dawn, all the nobles and lords came together; they performed the ritual dance in the same courtyard, and
18. with them the woman who was to die also danced, along with many other women adorned like her. The men went on their own side dancing in front, and the women went behind them.
19. It is said that while all were dancing thus, they arrived at the temple where that woman was to die. She was led up the steps. Once at the top, they laid her on someone's back,
20. and they cut open her chest, then drew out her heart and offered it to the sun. Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, etc.

On the Fixed Feasts. Folio 7

The ninth month was called Tlasochimaco. On the first day of this month they held a feast in honor of the god of war called Vitzilobuchtli; they offered him in it the first flowers of that year.

Chapter 9.

KL. Tlasochimaco

The night before this feast everyone was occupied with killing chickens and dogs to eat, and making tamales and other foods for the meal. Then, in the morning on the day of the feast, the priests of the idols adorned Vitzilobuchtli with many flowers. After the statue of this god was prepared, they also adorned the statues of the other gods, decking them with garlands, strings, and collars of flowers. They then dressed all the other statues in the neighborhood temples and young men's houses. In the houses of the tax-collectors, the nobles, and the common people, everyone adorned the statues they kept in their homes with flowers.

Once the statues of all the gods had been decorated, they all began to eat the food they had prepared the night before. And a little while after eating, they began a kind of dance: in this dance, noble men and women danced together, holding hands and linked to one another, with their arms placed around each other's necks. They did not dance in the manner of a professional dancer, nor did they make the movements of that style, but instead went step by step, to the sound of those who were playing and singing. These musicians were gathered a little apart from the dancers, near a round platform called the momutli.

This singing lasted until nightfall, not only in the courtyards of the temples but in all the houses of nobles and common people as well; they played and sang and made merry until night. Old men and old women drank pulque, but no young man or young woman drank it, and if any did, they were severely punished. Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, which are described at length elsewhere.

Book Two

The tenth month was called Xocotl Vetzi. On the first day of this month, they held a festival to the god of fire, called Xiuhtecutli or Ixcozauhqui. During this festival, they threw many slaves into the fire, bound hand and foot, and before they finished dying, they dragged them out of the fire to remove the heart before the image of this god.

Chapter 10

1 August, 13 days [remaining]
KL. Xocotl Vetzi — 2. Peter in Chains [feast day]

Day 3: During the festival of Nasochimaco, they went to the mountain and cut down a tree some twenty-five fathoms tall, and they dragged it to the courtyard of this god. There they stripped it of all its bark and raised it upright. It remained standing until the vigil of the feast, at which point they lowered it to the ground, using many ropes and devices so it would not crash down. On the vigil of this feast, early in the morning, many craftsmen and woodworkers came and smoothed it and made it very clean. After it was smoothed and prepared and decorated with many kinds of papers, they tied ropes and other cords to it and raised it with great shouts and loud noise, and fastened it securely.

Day 9: Once the pole or tree was bound and adorned with all its trappings, those who had slaves to throw alive into the fire began to adorn themselves with their feathers and finery, and they painted their bodies yellow, which was the livery of fire. Taking their captives with them, they danced and made celebration all that day until night.

Day 12: After keeping vigil all that night with the captives, and after performing many ceremonies with them, they sprinkled them with a powder called ycatehlli so that they would lose consciousness and not feel so much at the moment of death. They bound their hands and feet, and thus bound, they placed them on their shoulders and danced around the great post. Then came the moment of death. As they danced around, they threw the captives one by one onto the pile of burning coals. If one of them revived a little from the cold, and if the one who had been scorched was still alive, they let him burn for a good interval. And if he was still living and struggling, they pulled him out with some kind of hook and placed him on the sacrificial block. Opening his chest, they removed his heart. In this way all those wretched captives suffered.

Once the sacrifice described above was finished, all the young men rushed at it with great force. Many other ceremonies were performed as is written at length further on concerning this feast.

The eleventh month was called Ochpaniztli. On the first day of this month, they held a feast in honor of the mother of the gods, called Teteu Inna, or Hid, which means "our grandmother." They danced in honor of this goddess in silence, and they killed a woman in great silence, dressed in the adornments with which they depicted this goddess.

Chapter 11.
KL.    Ochpaniztli.

Five days before this month began, all the celebrations and festivities of the previous month ceased as this month commenced. They danced for eight days without singing and without the teponastli drum. When these days were over, the woman who represented the goddess they call Teteu Inna came out, adorned with the ornaments with which they depicted that same goddess, and a great number of women came out with her — especially healers and midwives. They went out and fought, pelting one another with bundles of pachili and with leaves of tinas, and with reeds made of cattail leaves and with flowers called compasochitl. This celebration lasted four days.

When these ceremonies and others of this kind were finished, they took care that the said woman should not understand that she was going to die, so that she would not weep or become sad, for they considered that a bad omen. When the night came on which she was to die, they brought her down very gently, making her understand that she was being taken to sleep with some great lord. They led her in great silence to the temple where she was to die. Once at the top, one man carried her on his back, back to back, and quickly they cut off her head and then flayed her, and a robust young man put on her skin.

He who wore the skin of the woman who had been killed was then taken with great solemnity, accompanied by many captives, to the temple of Huitzilopochtli. There, before Huitzilopochtli, four captives had their hearts removed, and the rest were left for the temple attendant to kill.

In this month the lord held a review of all the warriors, and all the young men who had not yet gone to war were given weapons and insignia and were enrolled as soldiers, so that from then on they would go to war.

Many other ceremonies were held before this feast, which are set down at length in its history.

3  c  On the fifteenth day of this month, the young men and boys swept all the altars and shrines of the gods — both those inside the houses and those along the roads and crossroads. For this service they were given ears of corn; some received a vessel full of corn, and others two or three ears.

On the eighteenth day, the god who is always a youth arrived — he was called Llamatyncatl [Tlamatzinocatl]. They said that because he was young and swift he traveled faster and arrived first. Then they offered food in his temple, and that night everyone ate and drank and made merry, especially the old men and old women who drank wine to celebrate the god's arrival; and they said they washed his feet with this rejoicing.

The last day of this month was the great festival, because they say all the gods arrived then. On the eve of that day, at night, they made on top of a mat of cornmeal a very dense little mound in the shape of a cheese. Into this mound the gods would press the print of a foot as a sign that they had arrived. All night the chief priest kept watch, going back and forth many times to look and see when he would find the footprint.

When the chief priest saw the sign of the footprint, he immediately shouted out, saying: "Our lord has arrived!" Then the priests of the temple began to blow trumpets, conch shells, and kettledrums, and other instruments they used at that time. As soon as the instruments were heard, all the people came to offer food at all the temples and shrines. Once again they made merry, washing the feet of their gods, as has been described above.

The following day, they said the old gods arrived last of all, because they moved more slowly on account of their age. This day had many adornments to make it more solemn. There were great piles of embers, and certain young men dressed as monsters danced around the fire; and while dancing they threw captives into the fire, in the manner described above.

Many other ceremonies were performed at this festival, as will be told further on.

The thirteenth month was called Tepeilhuitl. In this month they held a feast in honor of the prominent mountains that surround this region of New Spain, where storm clouds form. They made images in human form for each of those mountains from the dough called Tzoalli, and made offerings before these images in reverence to those very mountains.

Chapter 13

KL. Tepeilhuitl.

In honor of the mountains they made serpents of wood or of tree roots, and carved their heads to look like serpents. They also made thick wooden logs, long like a puppet, which they called Ecatotonti. Both these logs and the serpents they dressed with the dough called Tzoalli. These figures they fashioned in the manner of mountains, placing on top a head like a human head. They also made these images in memory of those who had drowned in the water or died in such a way that they were not cremated, but rather buried.

After observing many ceremonies and placing the said images on their altars, they offered them tamales and other foods, and they also sang songs in their praise and drank wine in their honor.

When the feast in honor of the mountains arrived, they killed four women and one man. One of the women was called Tepoxoth, the second Matlalquae, the third was called Sohtecatl, the fourth Mayauel, and the man was called Milnaouatl. They adorned these women and the man with many papers covered with rubber, and carried them on litters on the shoulders of richly dressed women, to the place where they were to be killed.

After they had killed them and removed their hearts, they sent the bodies rolling down the temple steps. When they reached the bottom, they cut off their heads and placed them on a pole. The bodies were taken to the houses called calpul, where they were divided up to be eaten. The papers with which the images of the mountains had been adorned, after being taken apart for the feast, were hung in the Calpul. Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, which are set down at length in its history.

The fourteenth month was called Quecholli. They held a feast for the god called Mixcoatl. In this month they made arrows and darts for war, and they killed many slaves in honor of this god.

Chapter 14

KL Quecholli

When they made the arrows over the course of five days, everyone bled themselves from the ears, and the blood they pressed from them they smeared on their own temples. They said they did this as penance in order to hunt deer. Those who did not bleed themselves had their cloaks tied around them as one. No man lay with his wife during these days, and neither old men nor old women used a walking stick, because they were doing penance.

When the four days of making arrows and darts were finished, they made certain arrows and small darts, and tied them in groups of four together with four torches. Having made a bundle of the four torches and the four arrows, they offered them on the graves of the dead. They also placed two tamales together with the arrows and torches. All of this remained on the grave for one full day, and at night they burned it. And they performed many other ceremonies for the dead during this same feast.

On the tenth day of this month, all the Mexicans and Tlatelolcans went to those mountains called Zacatepec. They say that mountain is their mother. On the day they arrived they made shelters or huts of grass, and they made fires, and they did nothing else that day.

The next day, as soon as dawn came, they all had a morning meal, and then they went out into the field and formed a great circle, surrounding many animals — deer, rabbits, and other animals — and little by little they drew the circle tighter until they had enclosed them all. Then they rushed in and each person caught whatever he could.

When the hunt was over, they killed captives and slaves at a temple called Llamatzinco. They bound their hands and feet and carried them up the steps of the temple, the way one drags a deer by its feet and hands. They killed them with great ceremony — both the man and the woman who represented the god Mixcoatl and his consort — at another temple called Mixcoteupan. And many other ceremonies followed.

The seventeenth month was called Tititl. In this month they held a feast for a goddess they called Tzcuítli, and by another name Yona, and by yet another name Cozcamiauh. In honor of this goddess they would kill a woman, and after removing her heart they would cut off her head and perform a ritual dance with it; the one who went in front carried the head by its hair in his right hand, making his dancing gestures.

Chapter 17.

KL. Tititl

The woman they killed for this feast was adorned with the garments of the goddess whose image she represented, who was called Flame-Tecuítli, and by another name Yona, which means "our mother." This woman, thus dressed in the garments described in the history, danced alone. Some old men provided the music, and as she danced she wept and sighed, remembering that she was soon to die. At midday, the priests dressed themselves in the ornaments of all the gods and went before her, leading her up to the temple where she was to die. She was cast upon the sacrificial stone, her heart was removed, and her head was cut off. Then one of those who had been going before her acting as a god, the foremost among them, took her head by the hair and performed the ritual dance with it — he led the way, carrying it in his right hand, making his dancing gestures with it. On that same day the ministers of the idols performed certain ceremonies, going up and down the temple steps one after another, carrying out certain rites. The following day all the common people made bags like purses, tied with cords about an arm's length long, and stuffed them with soft, wool-like materials. They hid these bags under their cloaks and would strike women who passed by in the street with them. This game went so far that boys also made the bags and beat girls with them until they made them cry. Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, which are described at length in the history of this feast.

They made an image of great craftsmanship that appeared to be surrounded by flames; and every four years during this same feast they killed slaves and captives in honor of this god. They also pierced the ears of all the children who had been born during those years, and godparents were assigned to them.

The feasts described above were fixed, always falling within the month or one or two days beyond. They also had movable feasts, which were observed according to the cycle of the twenty signs. These signs made a circuit of two hundred and sixty days; and therefore these movable feasts fell in one month one year and in another month the next year, and they always varied.

On the Movable Feasts.

The first movable feast was celebrated in honor of the sun, under the sign called Ce Ocelotl, in the fourth house called Naolmi. At this feast they offered quails to the image of the sun and burned incense; and at midday they killed captives before it in honor of the sun. On this same day everyone, young and old, bled themselves from the ears in honor of the sun and offered that blood to him.

The Second Movable Feast.

In this same sign, in the seventh house, all the painters held a feast. Certain embroiderers had fasted forty days — others twenty — to gain good fortune for painting well and weaving fine work. They offered quails and incense for this purpose, and the men performed other ceremonies to the god Chicome Xochitl and the women to the goddess Xochiquetzal.

Book Two

The Third Movable Feast.

In the third sign, which is called ce macatl: in the first house they held a feast for those called cioapipilti; because they said that at that time they descended to the earth, fanning their images with papers, and they offered offerings.

The Fourth Movable Feast

In the sign called ce macatl: in the second house called ymetochili: they held a great feast for the god called Ysguyteali, who is the second god of wine, and not only for him, but for all the gods of wine, who were many. On this day they adorned his image very well, and offered him food, and they sang and danced before him. In the courtyard of his temple they placed a great vat of pulque, and the tavern-keepers would fill it until it overflowed, and all who wished came to drink. They had reeds with which to draw from it; the tavern-keepers went about filling the vat so that it was always full. This was done chiefly by those who had newly cut the maguey plant. The first honey-water they extracted they brought to the house of this god as first-fruits.

The Fifth Movable Feast

In the sign called ce Xochitl: in the first house, the nobles and lords held a great feast; they danced and sang in honor of this sign, and held other celebrations. At that time they brought out the richest feather ornaments, with which they adorned themselves for the areito dance. And at this feast, the lord bestowed rewards upon the warriors, the singers, and the people of the palace.

The Sixth Movable Feast

In the sign called ce acatl: in the first house, the lords and nobles held a great feast for Quetzalcoatl, god of the winds. This feast was held in the house called calmecac, which was the house where the priests of the idols resided and where young men were raised. In this house, which was like a monastery, stood the image of Quetzalcoatl. On this day they adorned it with rich ornaments, and offered before it perfumes and food. They said that this was the sign of Quetzalcoatl.

The Seventh Movable Feast.

On the Moveable Feasts.
Folio 13.

In the sign called Ce Miquiztli: in the first house, the lords and nobles held a great feast for Tezcatlipoca, who was the great god. They said this was their fate, as all of them had oratories in their houses where they kept the images of this god and of many others. On this day they adorned this image, offered it perfumes, flowers, and food, and sacrificed quails before it, tearing off their heads. Not only the lords and nobles did this, but all the common people who came to know of this feast, and the same was done in the neighborhood temples and in all the great temples. Everyone prayed and asked this god to grant them favors, since he was all-powerful.

The Eighth Moveable Feast

In the sign called Ce Quiahuitl: in the first house, they held a feast for the goddesses called Cihuapipiltin. These were said to be the women who had died in their first childbirth; they were said to have become goddesses and to dwell in the house of the sun. When this sign reigned, they descended to earth and caused terrible diseases in those they encountered outside their homes. For this reason, during these days, no one dared leave their houses. Oratories had been built in honor of these goddesses at every crossroads in all the neighborhoods. These were called Cihuateocalli, or by another name Cihuateopan. In these oratories they kept images of these goddesses, and on these days they adorned them with papers called amateteuitl. During this feast, in honor of these goddesses, those condemned to death for some crime who were held in the jails were put to death.

The Ninth Moveable Feast.

In the sign called Ce Quiahuitl: in the fourth house, which was called Nahui Ehecatl, because this house was considered very ill-fated, criminals who were imprisoned were put to death. The lord also had certain slaves killed as an act of superstition. Merchants and traders made a display of the goods in which they dealt, bringing them out so that everyone could see them. Afterward, at night, they ate and drank, took flowers, and those canes of perfumes, and seated themselves in their...

...and each one began to boast of what he had won, and of the distant places he had traveled to, and he looked down on the others as being worth little, since they had not gone to as many distant places as he had. In this they had great laughter and mockery among themselves for a long stretch of the night.

The Tenth Moveable Feast

In the sign called Ce Malinalli, in the second house called Ome Acatl, they held a great feast. Because they said this sign belonged to Tezcatlipoca: in this feast they made the image of Omacatl, and anyone who had devotion to it would take it to their house, so that it would bless them and multiply their wealth. And when this happened, they kept it and did not want to let it go. Whoever wished to return this image would wait until the same sign came around again, and then they would take it back to where they had originally taken it from.

The Eleventh Moveable Feast

In the sign called Ce Tecpatl, in the first house they brought out all the ornaments of Huitzilobuchtli, cleaned them, shook them out, and set them in the sun. They said this was his sign, and also that of Camaxtli. This was done at Tlacateco. On this day they set out many kinds of food, very well prepared, as the lords eat it. All of it was presented before the image. After it had been there for a while, the officials of Huitzilobuchtli took it back and divided it among themselves and ate it. They also burned incense before the image and offered quail, beheading them in front of it, so that their blood would spill before the image. And the lord offered all the precious flowers that lords customarily use, before the image.

The Twelfth Moveable Feast

In the sign called Ce Ozomatli, they said that the goddesses called Cihuapipiltin descended to earth, and they struck boys and girls with palsy. And if anyone fell sick during this time, they said that those goddesses had caused it, because the person had encountered them. Parents during these days would not allow their sons or daughters to leave the house, so that they would not encounter these goddesses, of whom they had great fear.

Of the moveable feasts.

The thirteenth moveable feast.

In the sign they called Ce Itzuintli, they said it was the sign of fire. They held a great feast in honor of Xiuhteuctli, god of fire. At it, much copal was offered, and many quail. They adorned his image with many kinds of papers and with many rich ornaments. Among the wealthy and powerful, they held a great feast in honor of fire in their own homes. They held banquets and feasts in honor of fire. In this same sign they held the election of lords and consuls. And in the fourth house of this sign they celebrated the solemnity of their elections, with banquets, dances, and gifts. After these feasts they then publicly proclaimed war against their enemies.

The fourteenth moveable feast.

In the sign called Ce Atl, in the first house of this sign, they held a feast for the goddess of water, called Chalchiuhtlicue. All those who worked with water held the feast — whether selling water, fishing, or doing other trades that involve water. These people would compose her image, make offerings to it, and venerate it in the house called Calpulli.

The fifteenth common moveable feast.

Lords, nobles, prominent men, and wealthy merchants, when a son or daughter was born to them, paid great attention to the sign under which the child was born — the day and the hour of birth. They would then go to inform the astrologers and diviners, and inquire about the good or bad fortune of the newborn child. If the sign under which it was born was favorable, they would have it baptized right away. If it was unfavorable, they sought the most favorable house of that sign under which to baptize it. When they baptized the child, they invited relatives and friends to be present at the baptism, and on that occasion they gave food and drink to all present. They also baptized the children of the whole neighborhood. The baptism took place at sunrise, in the father's house, and the midwife baptized the child, saying many prayers and performing many ceremonies over the newborn. This feast is still practiced today at the baptisms of their children, insofar as the inviting, eating, and drinking are concerned.

The Sixteenth Movable Feast.

When the parents saw that their son was of age to marry, they would speak to him about wanting to find him a wife. He would respond, thanking them for the care they took in arranging his marriage. They then spoke to the principal officer who was in charge of all the young men, whom they called the Telpuchtlato, telling him that they wished to marry their son, and asking him to consider this a good thing. For this purpose they held a banquet for him and all the young men under his charge, and after giving them food and drink they made a speech to him and to all those under his charge. At the beginning of the speech, they placed before him an axe for cutting wood or timber. This axe was a sign that the young man was now taking leave of the company of the other young men, because they wished to marry him, and so the Telpuchtlato went away content. After this, the relatives among themselves decided upon the woman to be given to him, and they called upon the matchmakers, who were certain honorable old women, to go and speak to the girl's parents. They went two or three times, spoke with them, and returned with the answer. During this time the girl's relatives spoke among themselves, and agreeing to give her, they sent their consent to the matchmakers. After this they sought a well-fortuned day of some favorable sign, such as acatl, or cimalli, cipactli, or quauhtli. Having chosen one of these signs, the young man's parents informed the girl's parents of the day on which the marriage was to take place, and they then began to prepare all the necessary things for the wedding — food, drink, blankets, smoking reeds, and flowers. Having done this, they invited the leading men and all the other people they wished to have at the wedding. After the banquet and many speeches and ceremonies, people came on behalf of the young man to fetch her at nightfall. They carried her with great solemnity on the back of a matron, with many lit torches in two rows before her, and many people surrounding her, both behind and in front, until they arrived at the home of the young man's parents. Upon arriving at the young man's house, they placed both of them together beside the hearth, which they always kept burning in the middle of a room full of fire. The woman was placed to the left of the man. Then the young man's mother dressed her new daughter-in-law in a very fine huipil, and placed beside her feet some beautifully worked grinding stones. The girl's mother covered her new son-in-law with a very fine mantle, fastening it over his shoulder, and placed beside his feet a beautifully worked loincloth. the corner of the young man's cloak with the hem of the young woman's huipil. Thus the marriage was concluded, along with many other ceremonies, meals, drinks, and dances, which took place afterward, as is contained in the account of marriage.

They had two other feasts which were in part fixed and in part moveable: they were moveable because they were held in interpolated years. One was held every four years, and the other every eight years: they were fixed because they had a set year, month, and day. In the one held every four years, they pierced the ears of boys and girls, and performed for them the ceremonies of cueza for their well-being, and purified them by fire. In the one held every eight years, they fasted beforehand for eight days on bread and water, and performed a dance in which they took on the figures or personages of various birds and animals, and they said they were seeking fortune, as is written in the appendix of the second book.

These moveable feasts in some years displace the feasts of the Calendar, just as also happens in our own Calendar.

There is no need in this second book to provide a calculation of the ceremonies and idolatrous practices recounted in it, because they are in themselves so cruel and so inhumane that anyone who read them would be seized with horror and dread; and so I will do no more than set down the account plainly, word for word.

Quauitleoa: this feast day came about; and at that time, there in the mountains all around, the Tlaloque were honored; they came together and gathered at Tepetsinco, or else there at Velayhe.

Book Two: Of the Ceremonies.

On the first day of the first month of the year, which is called Quahuitlehua, and which the Mexicans called Atlcahualo, beginning on the second day of February: they held a great festival in honor of the gods of water, or of rain, called the Tlaloque. For this festival, they sought out many nursing infants, buying them from their mothers. They selected those who had two whorls of hair on their heads, and who had been born under a good sign, saying that these were the most pleasing sacrifice to these gods, so that they would send rain in its season. They took these children to be killed on the high mountains, where they had made vows to offer sacrifice. From some of them they removed their hearts, on those mountains; others were taken to certain places on the lake of Mexico. One place they called Tepetzinco, a well-known hill that stands in the lake; others were taken to another hill called Tepepulco, on the same lake; and others to the whirlpool of the lake called Pantitlan. Great numbers of children were killed each year in these places; after death they were cooked and eaten. During this same festival, in all houses and palaces, they raised poles like staves, on the tops of which they placed papers covered with drops of rubber; these papers they called amateteuitl: this they did in honor of the gods of water. The places where the children were killed are as follows. The first is called Quauhtepetl, an eminent hill that stands near Tlatelolco: to the boys or girls killed there, they gave the name of that same hill, Quauhtepetl. To those killed at Pantitlan: there they sent the divine image, and there also they erected the quauhtle, called cuenmantli, straight and slender, leaning only upon its own growth, and growing up from it. And there also they left the little children, dedicated to Tlacateteuhti: those among them who were of perfect sign; everywhere they were bathed and anointed: it was said that those who received them with joy, who welcomed them gladly, who rejoiced in them — theirs it was to go weeping, lamenting, calling for rain. And those who lived not in a calpan were offered at the young men's house and at Cacalpulco; everywhere they erected the slender, straight, dark-feathered paper banners fastened to them, dripping with rubber, spattered with rubber. And in several places at Quauhtepec: and those who died there, their image was also called Etiuia — of Quauhtepetl; their paper vestments were greenish-blue. At the second place of death, on top of the hill Ioaltecatl: its common name was Iciuh. Their vestment was that of Tlacateteuitl-Ioaltecatl; their paper garments were black and red and shining. At the third place, Tepetzinco: there a woman died, named Quetzalxoch, and they fastened to her the tepetzmitl, called [continues].

They dressed them with papers dyed crimson. The second mountain, upon which they killed children, is called Ioaltecatl; it is a prominent hill situated near Guadalupe. They gave the same name of the mountain to the children who died there, that is, Ioaltecatl. They dressed them with papers dyed black, with streaks of red ink. The third mountain, upon which they killed children, is called Tepetzino; it is that small hill which lies within this lagoon, facing Tlatelolco. The fourth mountain, upon which they killed children, was called Poiauhtlan. It is a mountain that lies on the borders of Tlaxcala, near Tepetzinco, on the eastern side. There they had built a house called Aiahcalli. In this house they killed children in honor of that mountain, and they called them Poiauhtla, like the mountain itself, which is over there on the borders of Tlaxcala. They dressed them with papers smeared with rubber oil. The fifth place where they killed children was the Zemelino, or sinkhole, of the lagoon of Mexico, which they called Pantitlan. Those who died there were called Epcoatl. The adornment with which they dressed them was an attire called Epnepaniuhqui. The sixth place, or mountain, where these children were killed is called Cocotl. It is a mountain situated near Chalco Atenco. The children killed there they called

In the fourth place, Poiauhtla Cantzintla, right at the foot of the mountain Tepetzino, the name given to those who died there was Poiauhtecatl; thus all was done as described above, in the manner called Vlpitabac, Tlauluitechti. In the fifth place, in the water, in the place called Pantitlan, those who died there were called Epcoatl. Their adornment was put on them as Epnepaniuhqui. They wore the chalchiuh necklace. They were adorned with izoluitl, and their faces were painted. And they wore the molcac garment. All were honored and completely adorned in full regalia, all bent low, all bowing before them.

They called them "coatl," just as the mountain itself was called, and they dressed them with papers, half red and half tawny. The seventh place where they killed the children was a mountain called Yiauhqueme, which is near Atlacujoaia; they gave them the name of that same mountain and adorned them with papers dyed in a tawny color. The poor children, before they were taken to be killed, were adorned with precious stones, with rich feathers, and with very elaborate and finely worked garments and sandals, also very finely worked. They put paper wings on them like angels, and they anointed their faces with rubber ointment, and in the middle of their cheeks they placed a small white disk. They placed them on very well-adorned litters, with rich feathers and other rich jewels. Carrying them on the litters, they went along playing flutes and trumpets as they customarily did. Everywhere the children were carried, all the people wept. When they arrived with them at an oratory that stood near Tepetzinco on the western side, which they called Tocooan, there they kept them all night long, watching, and the priests of the idols sang songs so that the children would not sleep. And when they were taking the children to the places where they were to be killed, if they went along crying and shedding many tears, those who saw them cry gathered around, because they said it was a sign that it would rain soon. And if they encountered a dropsical person on the road, they considered it a bad omen and said such a person was preventing the rain. If any of the ministers of the temple, and others called Quaquacujlti, and the elders turned back to their homes and did not go to where they were to kill the children:

They adorned them with papers on their backs, with amate paper, paper decorations; they placed them on litters adorned with quetzal feathers, and there upon them they stood erect, with fine feather work, all embellished and made to weep greatly, with deep sighing. And when they arrived at Tocooan, at the place called Aiauhecalco, there a house was assigned to them. And the little children who were being watched — if their faces showed tears streaming down, if their faces showed tears dropping, it was said and proclaimed that it would rain; their tearful faces were taken as a sign of rain, their tears made hearts glad and they said: now the rain will come, now it will be that rain will begin. And if one turned back, they said he had abandoned the task. Quickly then [the priests] would come running: now they would finish and complete it; immediately then the screech owls came, and also...

They held them to be infamous and unworthy of any public office; from that point forward they were called mocauhque, which means the abandoned ones. They took omens from the rain, and from the frost of the year, from the arrival of certain birds, and from their songs. They performed another cruelty at this same feast: all the captives were taken to a temple they called Topico, of the god Totec. In this place, after many ceremonies, they tied each one of them upon a stone like a millstone, and bound them so that they could walk all around the circumference of the stone. They gave them a wooden sword without blades, and a shield, and placed pieces of pine wood before them to throw; and the same ones who had captured them came to fight with them, with swords and shields, and upon knocking them down, they immediately took them to the place of sacrifice, where they were thrown on their backs upon a stone three or four palms high and a palm and a half wide in square, which they called techcatl. Four men held them — two by the feet and two by the arms — and another held the head, and another with a flint blade, with one blow struck them through the chest; and through that opening he put his hand and pulled out the heart, which he then offered to the sun and to the other gods, pointing it toward the four parts of the world. After this was done, they threw the body down the steps, and it rolled down, hitting the stairs until it reached the bottom; upon reaching the bottom, the one who had captured him claimed it, and having cut it into pieces, he distributed it to be eaten cooked.

They cried out, calling upon one another, saying that nowhere did they appear, nowhere did they show themselves, that all those around the temalacac stone — that in just this way one would die — they called out to prepare them for the quavitleoa ceremony before all: they were to go to the place of Totec; there they would select them well, as they were about to die, and slaughter them: they would only select them well; they gave them iotlaxcalli or iopitlaxcalli bread, and thus slaughtered them. And four times they appeared before witnesses, four times they were drawn out, stripped, made known: they gave them food, they fed them the nechichioal drink: the first time it was offered, the first time they were suckled, it was colored red, it went becoming red. It was strong, the red drink. The second time it was white, the nechichioal drink. The third time, once again the same drink came upon them reddish. The fourth time, white: they completely covered them with it, they completely bathed them in it, they carried it so that it would fall upon their task, so that they would speak harshly, so that their breath would come out, so that they would be scratched: [continues]

Exclamation of the author. —

I do not believe there is a heart so hard that, upon hearing of a cruelty so inhuman, and more than bestial and diabolical, as that described above, it would not be moved to tenderness, tears, horror, and astonishment. And it is certainly a lamentable and terrible thing to see that our human nature has fallen to such lowness and disgrace: that fathers, at the suggestion of the devil, would kill and eat their own children (without thinking they were committing any offense whatsoever) but rather thinking that in doing so they were rendering great service to their gods. The fault for this so cruel blindness, which was carried out upon these unfortunate children, ought not to be attributed so much to the cruelty of the fathers — who shed many tears and carried it out with great sorrow in their hearts — as to the most cruel hatred of our most ancient enemy Satan, who with his most malignant cunning persuaded them to such an infernal deed. O Lord God, render justice against this cruel enemy, who does us so much harm and desires to do us more: strip him, Lord, of all his power to harm.

They took their adornments and no longer exchanged them, no longer replaced them; and with them they adorned themselves with the marking cord. And those who were draped and hung, those who were in ill condition, those who were afflicted; they became parched, they became withered, they became enraged in their souls, their feet became white and stiff. ¶ This is the third chapter, which speaks of the marvelous ceremonies and the penitential rites which they performed during the very first month called Tlacaxipeoaliztli.

Of the festival                    Tlacaxipeoaliztli.    fo. 18.

On the last day of the said month, they held a very solemn festival in honor of the god called Xipe Totec, and also in honor of Huitzilopochtli. In this festival, they killed all the captives — men, women, and children. Before killing them, they performed many ceremonies, which are as follows. On the eve of the festival, after midday, they began a very solemn ceremony, and they kept vigil throughout the night — those who were to die — in the house called calpulco. There they pulled out the hair from the crown of their heads. Near the fire they performed this ceremony; they did this at midnight, when they customarily drew blood from the ears to offer to the gods, which they always did at midnight. At dawn, they led them to where they were to die, which was the temple of Huitzilopochtli. There the ministers of the temple killed them in the manner described above, and they flayed all of them. For this reason they called the festival Tlacaxipeoaliztli, which means "the flaying of men." Those who were flayed were called xipeme, and by another name, tototecti. The first name means "the flayed ones." The second means "those who died in honor of the god Totec." The owners of the captives handed them over to the priests at the foot of the temple pyramid, and the priests led them up by the hair, each one his own, up the steps. And if any captive was unwilling to go of his own accord, they dragged him along...

[Nahuatl column:] Tlacaxipeoaliztli: this was the festival that fell at this time. And the reason it was observed was because at that time all the captives would die — all the male slaves, all the female slaves, and all the children. Those who owned them — their death was to come the next day; when the sun began to rise and when it climbed up — and all that night, in the calpulco, they combed their hair and lifted their faces up. Indeed at that time they were set in place, when the night was divided, at the place of piercing. And there they caused them to bleed, as they were about to die; they spent all that day — and indeed all that full day — everyone was flaying them, carrying out the flaying. Thus it was called Tlacaxipeoaliztli. And those captives called xipeme and tototecti — those who were being killed were the sacrificial officiants. It was not the owners themselves who watched over them; they only set guards over them, placed them in the guards' hands, had them escorted down, held them at their sides, carried them on their backs, so that they brought them up to the top of the temple. And if a captive was truly grieving and very faint of heart, because he was about to fall, they would lift him up and carry him along; and if a captive was truly firm...

[This may be tedious for the reader, though all of these things are explained in the [Nahuatl] language.] During this festival they held certain games, which were the following: all the skins of the flayed men were worn by many young men, who were called tototecti. They all sat down upon beds of hay or plaster or chalk, and while seated there, other young men provoked them to fight, either with words or with pinches. And those who had been provoked would chase after the ones who had incited them; and the others would run, and when caught, they would begin to wrestle or fight, one against another; and they would capture one another, and they would lock up the prisoners, and they could not leave the jail without paying something. When this fight was over, they then began to knife those who were to die by knife wounds, upon the grinding stone. Four men fought against these condemned ones — two dressed as jaguars and two as eagles. And before they began to fight, they would raise the shield and the sword toward the sun, as if asking the sun for strength; and then they would begin to fight, one against one, and if the captive was brave and defended himself well, two would attack him, then three, and if he still defended himself, all four would attack him in this fight; and they would go dancing and making many movements, all four of them.

[Nahuatl column:] In the calpulco, where he had vowed, or had promised, or had pledged himself: they would take him, and bring him to his home, and those who would eat him — they would scrape him, pound him, grind him, shell him. But first Moctezuma received one [portion], one thigh, which went to him as his due. And the captor was given gifts; and his companions were summoned, they were gathered together, so that the captive's household would be feasted. They would give him a full basinfull of maize grain, the one called tlacatlaelli, and upon it went dried whole ears of corn, called tonaluh, ticatl, huiztli — because in this way all the things of the captor would be [honored]. And they would name it "the sun-greeting," and the food and drink of the captor had all been done: so that he would not go to war and be killed there, and so that he would not go being deceived, so that the weeping salutation of the others, those who had been his captives, would be done. And on the next day at dawn — when it became day, when the night ended, when the night released them — when dawn broke, the captives were made to go, those being led; and those who led them around: they would finish again at midnight, for it was said that the Quauhtecatl had been caught, since in that very spot he had been defeated, and from there he faced and gazed upon the rising sun, and there he lay before the sun.

And then a priest would come, with a quail, and he would wring off its head, twisting it off in front of the captive who was to die. And then that same priest would take the shield of the captive and raise it up high. And then the quail, whose head had been cut off, he would throw it behind him. Having done this, they then made the captive climb up onto the round stone, shaped like a millstone. And while the captive was on the stone, one of the priests or ministers of the temple would come, dressed in a bear skin. He served as a kind of godfather to those who died there, and he would take a rope, which came out through the hole in the millstone, and he would tie it around the captive's waist. Then he would give him his wooden sword, which, in place of obsidian blades, had bird feathers glued along its edge, and he gave him four pine clubs with which to defend himself and to throw at his opponents. The owner of the captive, having left him in the manner already described upon the stone, would go to his own place, and from there he would watch what happened with his captive, while dancing. Then those who were prepared for the fight would begin to fight with the captive, one by one. Some captives who were brave would exhaust all four of them, fighting. And they could not make him surrender. Then a fifth would come, who was left-handed, and who used his left hand as his right. This one

would taunt him with his shield device. And then, from behind him they rushed him. Then they seated him on top of the sacrificial stone. Chapter six, concerning the feast that was held at the Kalends of the fifth month, which was called Toxcatl.

The fifth month was called Toxcatl. In this month they held a feast and celebration in honor of the principal god called Tescatlipuca, who was also known by the name Titlacaoan, and by another name Iautl, and by another Telpochtli, and by another Tlamatsinctl. In this feast they killed a young man of very fine appearance, whom they had raised for the space of one year in pleasures, saying that he was the image of Tescatlipuca. Upon killing the young man who had been raised for one year, they immediately placed another in his place, to be raised for the space of one year. Of these they kept many in reserve, so that one would immediately succeed the one who had died. They chose them from among all the captives, the most handsome men. The calpixques kept them under guard and took great care that they should be the most able and best disposed that could be found, and without any bodily defect whatsoever.

This is the sixth chapter, which speaks of the feast called Ilhujtl, and of the nextlaoalli that took place during the one-day feast of the fifth month, which was called Toxcatl.

During Toxcatl, it was a very great feast of Tescatlipuca. There he appeared, there he was honored; it was there that he was worshipped and that the image of him that had lived for one year died. And then another image was immediately set up. And this one lived for another year as his representative, kept by the calpixques who maintained his representatives. Perhaps ten of them lived at a time. They were well fed and fattened. And when they came forth, the captives were selected from among them — whoever was in good health and well formed in body. Then the calpixques took them and kept them. And at the proper time they raised up the one who was to represent him; the others served as replacements. Those selected were well-formed in appearance, knowing, discerning, of clean skin, not rough, not thin, not overly large, not too small, not too tall, reed-like in form, rounded like a cylinder, not flabby of body, not fat, not too small, not too large of frame; their appearance was...

¶ Chapter Seven: of the feast and sacrifices that were performed at the Kalends of the sixth month, which was called Etzalqualiztli.

The sixth month they called Etzalqualiztli: in this month they held a feast in honor of the gods of water, or of rain, whom they called tlaloque. Before this feast arrived, the priests of the idols fasted four days. And before beginning the fast, they went for rushes to a spring located near the town called Cristaltepec, because there grow very large and very thick rushes, which they call aztapilin, or tol—

And on the day of the feast, the common people made etzalli, they prepared it, they truly poured it out together if they did not prepare the etzalli: and when it was done, then they ate it together, they gave it to one another, and they greeted each other with it. And some who were joyful went about in gladness: and also some masqueraders went about making merry, going around from house to house rattling their cane-sticks, receiving etzalli: they went about carrying their xocujolli pots, their etzal-pots. Thus they said when they went about receiving: "Listen, listen — give me some etzalli, if you do not give it to me, I will smash your gourd-vessel." And when the householder heard this, he immediately gave them a full bowl of etzalli, handing over the etzalli bowl: some gave five, some six, some seven, and so they went about receiving. A kind of penance: they called this feather "quetzalmjaoaiud." Once they were arranged in this manner, they sounded the trumpets and conch shells, and then they began to go along their road. This procession was made to bring those who had committed some offense, of those mentioned before, to the place where they were to be punished. And so they led them as prisoners in this procession; they held them by the hair of their forelocks, so that none of them would flee. They held them by the loincloths they wore wrapped around them. And the little sacristan boys, who had also committed some offense, were carried upon the shoulders of these others, seated on a small seat made of green rushes. The other boys, who were the overseers, held them by the hand, leading them to the water where they were to be punished. They threw them into the water wherever they found a lagoon along the road, and they mistreated them with stones, blows, and kicks, and they threw them and rolled them in the mud of whatever lagoon was along the road. In this manner they led them to the edge of the water where they were to be cast in, which they called "toteco." Upon arriving at the edge of the water, the priest and the other ministers burned paper as a sacrifice, and the forms of copal that they carried, and the images of rubber, and they cast incense into the fire; and others spread it around over the rush mats with which that place was adorned. Together with this, those who brought the offenders threw them into the water, whose splashing made a great noise in the water, and the water rose up high on account of those who fell into it. And those who came up to the surface were [made to go back]...

In the seventh month, called Tecuilhuitontli, in this month they held a feast and sacrifices to the goddess of salt, whom they called Vixtocihuatl, who was the goddess of those who make salt. They said she was the sister of the gods of rain, and because of a certain misfortune that occurred between them, they persecuted her and banished her to the salt waters, and there she invented salt, in the way it is still made today, using pans and heaping up salted earth; and for this invention, those who dealt in salt honored and worshipped her. The attire of this goddess was yellow in color, with a miter adorned with many green feathers that stood out from it, like tall plumes stirred by the wind.

And this Vixtocioatl goes in the middle; one carries a reed staff leading her, and one old man carries her upon his back: and this staff is called Vixtopetlacotl. And this Vixtocioatl sang daily in the women's courtyard, until ten days were completed: and when the ten days arrived, in the late afternoon they began to sing for her, making her sing throughout the whole night; she never slept, they caused drowsiness to come upon her, so the night fell. And they made Vixtocioatl dance, holding her, the old women walked about making her dance: likewise all that night the captives who were to die the next day also danced, as they were destined to be laid out, as they would be covered over. And when dawn came, when the feast day had truly arrived, then those who would offer the sacrifice adorned themselves, those who were to sacrifice: these were called Vixtoti; they dressed themselves as owls (vixtoti), they put on their ritual attire, their painted designs of the sweeping ceremony (ochpaniztli), and their paper arm-bands: and this was their headdress, the eagle-feather crest.

They carried lighted torches before them as they went dancing: these torches were carried by certain young soldiers, trained in war, who were called telpochtequioaque. These torch-bundles were heavy, and made those who carried them stoop over, as the resin dripped and embers fell from the torches: and sometimes some of the burning torches would fall. On either side, from one part and the other, they went giving light with torch-holders called tlemaitl. These were carried by young men who, by their vow, did penance for twenty days in the temple: those on one side were from Tenochtitlan, and those on the other side were from Tlatelolco. These did not dance; they only went about giving light, and watched carefully to see if anyone committed an indecency, by looking at or touching some woman.
