One of these places is called Tetamaçolco, another is called Necocyxecan, another is called Atenchicalcan, and the fourth is called Xolloco. These four places, where the offerings were made, corresponded in reverence to the four signs of the count of years: the first is called Acatl, which means "reed"; the second is called Tecpatl, which means "flint," like the iron head of a lance; the third is called Calli, which means "house"; and the fourth is called Tochtli, which means "rabbit." With these four signs, going around in turn, until each one of them completed thirteen years, they reckoned the count of years, up to fifty-two. In the tenth month, called Xocotl huetzi: once the feast of Hasuchimaco had passed, they would cut down a great tree in the mountains, twenty-five fathoms in length. Once everyone had gathered, they bound it with ropes, and having made a hole where it was to be set upright, they all pulled on the ropes, and they raised the tree amid great shouting. They filled in the hole with stones and earth so that it would remain standing, and thus it remained for twenty days. On the eve of the feast called Xocotl Huetzi, they would little by little let it fall to the ground, taking care that it not strike down hard, so that it would not break or split; and thus they would go about receiving it with some timbers tied together in pairs, called cuauhtomatl, and they would lay it upon the ground without its suffering any damage, and they would leave it so. In the ninth month, they called it Ochpaniztli: the first five days of this month they did nothing regarding the feast. After the five days had passed, fifteen days before the feast they began to dance a dance that they called Nematlaxo. This dance lasted eight days. They went arranged in four rows and danced in this dance; they did not sing, but went along walking and in silence, and they carried in both hands flowers called cempoalxochitl, not arranged, but cut with the stem itself. Some mischievous young men, though the others went in silence, made with their mouths the sound that the drum made, to whose sound they danced. They made no movement with their feet nor with their body, but only with their hands, lowering them and raising them in time with the drum. They kept the order with great care, so that no one would differ from another. They began this dance toward evening, and it ended at sunset. This lasted for eight days, at the end of which the women — healers, young girls, and old women — then began to carry out a skirmish, or fight, many and varied, in two squadrons. The women did this in front of that woman who was to die in this feast, in order to cheer her up, so that she would not be sad nor weep, for they held it to be a bad omen.

[The Nahuatl text parallels the Spanish account of the tenth feast called Ochpaniztli, describing how it was not yet time to perform the full ceremony until the days had been completed; it tells of the preparation period, the arrangement of participants in rows, the carrying of cempoalxochitl flowers bound together, the orderly, silent procession and dance accompanied by the sound of the drum, performed with great care and uniformity among the participants, each keeping to his place without disorder, continuing for the appointed days before the next part of the ceremony began.]

...they called them thus, because in this month the thunder usually began, and the first rains fell there, in the mountains: and the common people said, "now the Tlaloque gods are coming." At this time the priests of the Tlaloques went about very devout and very penitent, praying to their gods for water and awaiting the rain, as it began to thunder and give signs of rain. Then these priests took their censers, which were like great perforated spoons, full of coals, with long, thin, round, and hollow handles, which had rattles inside them, and the end of which was a serpent's head. Into these censers, over the coals, they threw their incense, which they call yiauhtli; and they began at once to make noise with the rattles that were on the handle, shaking it this way and that, and then they began to cense all the statues of the temples and of the tlaxilacalli (ward shrines). With these services they petitioned for and awaited the rain. The other people, for love of water, made vows to fashion the images of the mountains: five days before this feast arrived, they bought paper, rubber, henequen fiber, and razors; and with great devotion they prepared themselves with fasting and penance to make the images of the mountains, and to cover them with paper. Although they bathed, they did not wash their heads, only their necks: the men abstained from the women, and the women from the men. The night of the vigil of the feast, to await the dawn of the feast of Atemuztli — which fell on the twentieth day of this month — they spent the whole night cutting papers into various shapes. These papers, cut in this way, were called teteuitl, "cut ones." These papers they stuck onto large poles, from bottom to top, in the manner of a banner. All these papers were stained with rubber (ulli); and afterward each one set up this pole in the courtyard of his own house, and there it remained for the whole day of the feast. And those who had made the vow to make the images invited the ministers of the idols to come to their houses to make the papers with which they were to adorn the images of the mountains; and they made these in their monastery, called the calmecac. After this had been done, they carried [the images] to the houses of those who had made the vow; and they also carried their teponaztli drum, their rattles, and the tortoise shell to play upon. On arriving, they then arranged the images that had been made,

They also said that all the rest of the year they wore out the sustenance, "opan," because they mixed it with salt, lime, and saltpeter: and thus they dressed and undressed it in various garments, by which it became worn and aged. And with this fast, it was renewed: and the day after the fast, it was called "molpalolo," which means: they ate other things besides bread, because by then it had become something to be respected (sacred/penitential).

And [concerning] the women and the old men who were called by that name, the Macateca, there they swallowed the snakes, while they were still alive, moving and writhing; they seized them only with their mouths, not with their hands; rather they held them with their knees, so as to take them from the water there before Tlaloc: and as soon as they had swallowed the snakes, the Macateca danced because of this. And whoever was first to finish swallowing the snake which he had swallowed, then cried out loudly, giving a shout, and went to the temple: and they gave him gifts, to those who had swallowed the snakes: and for two days there was dancing, three times they circled around the temple four times. And then the xocotamalli (fruit tamales) were eaten, which filled the maize bins: all the people took them, when the feast ended. And the old women and old men who were there wept greatly, remembering that they might not live to see another eight years; they said: "Will this happen again? Our sustenance is now going to rest for eight years, because, it is said, we greatly afflict it, in that we grind it, we pound it, we crush it, we mash it with lime; as if we were putting it to death bit by bit in order to give ourselves life by it: it is said that it is now going away, taking with it, as it were, its children, which are our sustenance, and..."

The seventh building, or cu, was called Tlaxico: in this cu they killed every year a captive in honor of the god of the underworld; they killed him in the month called Titil. The eighth building was called Quauhxicalco; it was an oratory where the lord withdrew to do penance and fast. When this was done, a fast was held called netonatiuhqualo: they fasted four days in honor of the sun. This fast was held every two hundred and three days. And here they killed four captives, who were called chachanme; and two other captives, called the images of the sun and the moon, along with many other captives, last of all.

The ninth building was called Tochinco; it was a low cu, square in shape, with stairs on all four sides. Here they killed every year the image of Ome Tochtli, and when this sign reigned, this image was a captive adorned with the ornaments of the god of wine, who is called Ome Tochtli.

The tenth building was called Teotlalpan, which means "rugged land"; it was a small grove enclosed by four walls, like a corral, in which there were artificial crags made by hand, and planted with the kind of shrubs that grow on rugged ground, such as small magueyes and others called tzioactli. In this little grove they held a procession every year, in the month called Quecholli; and once the procession was finished, then

And there died those called chachanme, only four of them; and there also died the images of the sun and of the moon; and also very many captives died there. And this took place only afterward.

And when she had died, then they flayed her; and at dawn the fire priest put on her skin, that of Chicomecoatl; then three times he went in procession, he circled the eagle vessel, he danced; and this was done every year, in [the month of] Ochpaniztli.

¶ Centzontotochtin Inteopan.
In Centzontotochtin Inteopan there died Tepuztecatl, and Totoltecatl, and Papaztac; and those who died there [did so] not at night, but by day, in [the month of] Tepeilhuitl; and this was done every year.

¶ Cinteupan.
In Cinteupan there was [a place], there was kept the image of Cinteotl; there died the image of Cinteotl, on one day.

¶ Netotiloian.
In Netotiloian there danced those who had been bathed [i.e., the sacrificial victims], those of the nine winds, when they were about to die; and when they died it was at midnight, not by day.

The sixty-second building was called Temalacatl: it was a stone, like a great millstone, and it was pierced in the middle, like a millstone. Upon this stone the slaves were placed, and they fought each other with knives, tied by the middle of the body in such a way that they could reach to the edge of the stone, and they were given the weapons with which to fight. This was a very frequent spectacle, which drew crowds from all the surrounding regions to watch: a priest dressed in a skin of a bear or of a wolf/jaguar [cuetlachtli] stood there as godfather of the captives who were to be killed there; he brought them to the stone, tied them there, gave them their weapons, and wept for them while they fought. And when the captive fell, he handed him over to the one whose task it was to cut out his heart — another priest, dressed in a different skin, who was called Yohuallahuan ("Night Drinker").
This account is written at greater length in the account of the feast of Tlacaxipehualiztli.

Of Xiuhtecutli: there they took the fire, when Moctezuma offered incense, and there the fire was kindled: once a year, at the feast of Oauhquitamalqualiztli.

1. The Temalacatl.

This is the Temalacatl: there the captives were striped with paint, there they painted them with stripes, gathering many captives there; and thus they were painted, and all the people came from everywhere to witness the killing there at the temalacatl. And there it was the duty of the one dressed as the wolf/jaguar to throw down the captive at the temalacatl. And when he had thrown down the captive, then they gave him the war club, and gave him a feathered club. Then his counterpart went forth to fight him: either one attired as an eagle or as an ocelot; then they fought with the captive as if making war. And there it was the duty of the one called Chalchiuhtepehua. And when the captive fell, then the one dressed as the wolf/jaguar dragged him away; then they cut open his chest; and the one who performed the killing, whose name was Yohuallahuan, cut open the chest. And when they had cut open the captive's chest, then they carried him down below; and all this took place once a year, during the feast of Tlacaxipehualiztli.

In Coatlan, there died those called the Centzonhuitznahua: either when the burden-offering was made, or when the feast of Quecholli arrived, once a year.

The seventy-fourth building was called Atempan: it was a house where they gathered the children who were to be killed, and also the lepers, called xixioti, who were likewise killed. After having gathered them, in this place they carried them in procession on litters. This done, they took them to the places where they were to be killed.

The seventy-fifth building was called Tezcacoac Tlacochcalco: it was a house where many darts were kept, and many arrows stored for the time of war. Here they sacrificed slaves as an offering of devotion for some years.

The seventy-sixth building was called Acatl Yiacapan Vei Calpulli: this was a house where they gathered the slaves who were to be killed in honor of the Haloque (rain spirits); and after they were dead, they immediately cut them into pieces and cooked them. The seventy-seventh building was called Techielli; it was a small enclosure: here they offered reeds called acxoyatl.

Of Atenpan.

At Atempan, there they gathered together the lords [or offered the "lord of the earth"]; and once they had gathered them, they then went in procession, carrying them along the way. And when they had taken them in procession, they then went and bathed them, either in the water at the foot of the hill, or on top of the mountain, clothed as rain-bringers.

Of Tezcacoac Tlacochcalco

At Tezcacoac Tlacochcalco, there they bought [arms], only at certain times, when there was a great gathering of captives; and there the darts and arrows were kept, for the purpose of conquest.

Of Acatl Yiacapan, the great calpulli.

At Acatl Yiacapan, the great calpulli, there they gathered together all the Haloque [rain-spirit impersonators]; and when they had gathered them, they then killed them there. And when they had killed them, they then cut them into pieces there, and cooked them, and with this they celebrated the feast of the squash blossoms. And when they had cooked them, the noble youths ate them, as did all the lords; but the commoners did not eat of them — only the lords did.

Of Techielli

At Techielli, there the ritual offering of pine branches (acxoyatl) was made.

The seventy-eighth building was called calpulli: these were small houses, all enclosed around the patio on the inside. These small houses were called calpulli: here all the principal men and officials of the community gathered to fast and do penance for four days, [during] the vigils of the feasts that occurred every twenty days. Thus they observed the vigil for four days: and during this fast some ate at midnight, and others at midday.

Account of the Mexicans concerning the things that were offered in the temple.

Calpulli.

All the small houses stood in rows, surrounding the temple; it was called calpulli, the place where fasting was done. Only the noblemen, the rulers, the elders, and the officials fasted there; it was said that for twenty days they fasted, five days at a time. And when they fasted, it was five days before the feast arrived; and only at that feast did the period of fasting end. In this way they fasted, abstaining from food: some ate at midday and continued until midnight; others, who ate at midnight, continued until midday — thus it was reckoned. And when they fasted it lasted five nights, not five full days, only the nights: when night fell, they went in [to fast]; and when it dawned, they came out and went to their labors. Thus they did each day until the five days were completed; and during this time they no longer had relations with women.

Here is told what things were offered, and what was offered in this temple, among the Mexica.

...where they would enter some place where there were images of the idols: one, or many. They then touched the ground with their finger, and then raised it to the mouth, or to the tongue; this they called "eating earth," and they did it in reverence of their gods. And all those who left their houses, even if they did not leave the town, upon returning home, did the same; and along the roads, whenever they passed in front of some temple or shrine, they did the same. And in place of an oath, they used this same gesture: to affirm that what they said was true, they performed this ceremony. And those who wanted to be satisfied about what someone had said — if it was true what he spoke — would ask him to perform this ceremony, and then they believed him, as if it were an oath.

They had another ceremony, commonly practiced, which they called tlatlaçaliztli, meaning "a throwing": it consisted of no one eating without first throwing into the fire a small morsel of what he was about to eat.

They had yet another ceremony, also common, that no one was to drink pulque without first spilling a little at the edge of the hearth. And whenever someone opened a jar of pulque, they would first pour some of it into a basin, and place the basin near the fire, and from there take it with a cup, and pour it out to

the devil, or in front of the hearth: and in this way it was confirmed, in this way the words were made true: whenever something was not much believed to be true, it was told; if it were true what he said, he would say "throw it into the fire so it may be eaten"; thus at once it was believed, confirming that person's word.

The Throwing Ceremony (Tlatlaçaliztli).

And thus was performed the tlatlaçaliztli: when something was about to be eaten, before it was eaten — whether it was food — first a small little bit was broken off and thrown toward the hearth; there it was cast. Once it had been thrown, then eating would begin: no one ate first without first having thrown his offering toward the hearth.

The Pouring Ceremony (Tlatoyahualiztli).

Thus was performed the tlatoyahualiztli: when pulque was drunk, or honey-wine was drunk; when someone for the first time set out pulque, when it had just been tapped, when it was announced, a basin was brought out and placed in front of the hearth, along with a small drinking vessel. Neztlavaliztli.

This neztlavaliztli ritual was performed by anyone to whom something, such as an illness, had happened upon him, or who had been healed of a sickness; then he would burn copal and paper, as a penance, so that he would not die—as if he were thereby repaying a debt, since he had nearly died.

Those who escaped from some illness, on the advice of some astrologer, would choose a well-fortuned day. On that day, inside their house, they would burn in the hearth many papers upon which the astrologer had painted, with rubber [ulli], the figures of those gods who they supposed had helped them recover from the illness. The astrologer gave these papers to the one making the offering, telling him: "This is the god that is painted there," and then the other would throw the paper into the fire; and once all the papers were burned, they would gather the ashes and bury them in the patio of the house. This they called neztlahualiztli.

Every day in the world, they offered blood and incense to the sun, as soon as it rose in the morning. They offered it blood from their ears, and blood from quails: and tearing off the heads of these, with the blood running, they raised them toward the sun, as if offering it that blood. And doing this, they said: "The sun has now risen, he who is called Tonameh, Xiuhpiltontli, Quauhtleoanitl: we do not know how he will accomplish his course this day; we do not know whether some misfortune will befall the people."

And then they addressed their words to the sun itself, saying: "Our Lord, perform your office prosperously." This was done every day, at sunrise. They offered it incense four times each day, and five times at night. Once at sunrise, another time at the hour of terce, another at midday, and the fourth time at sunset. At night they offered incense: the first time when it was already fully dark; the second time, when everyone was about to go to sleep; the third time, when the bell began to ring for people to rise for matins; the fourth time, a little after midnight; the fifth time, a little before dawn broke. And when they offered incense at the first part of the night, they greeted the night, saying: "The lord of the night has now arisen, he who is called Yoaltecutli: we do not know how his office or his course will go." The feast of this Yoaltecutli fell and was celebrated on the sign called Vi Ollin, two hundred and three days into the count of the Tonalamatl. Four...

Every day, when the sun rose, there was the cutting of quail (sacrifice) and the burning of incense. And in the cutting of the quail, they severed the neck of the bird, and offered it, raising it toward the sun, and reddened it (with blood) as an offering. They said: "The sun has now arrived, he who is Tonameh, Xiuhpiltontli, Quauhtleovanitl. And however his day's course shall go, whatever may happen under his guidance and protection, may it be fulfilled. Perform your duty, perform your service, O our lord." And thus was done each day when the sun rose, as has been said. And as for the offering of incense, it was done four times by day and five times by night. The first time was when the sun appeared; the second time was at mealtime; the third time was at midday; the fourth time was when the sun was setting. And at night, the offering of incense was likewise made: the first time at nightfall; the second time at the hour when people go to sleep; the third time at the sounding of the trumpets (for prayer); the fourth time at the hour the priests keep watch; and the fifth time near dawn. And when it grew dark, the incense-burning and greeting were performed, saying: "Now comes Yoaltecutli, his staff (or his burden) arrives, and how will his task turn out?" And on his feast day...

On the feast of the sun, which fell on [the day] Four Movement, which occurred every two hundred and eight days, fasting and prayer were observed, and for four days there was abstinence from food [certain fasting]. And on the day the feast arrived, at midday, flutes were played and incense was offered. The small children who dwelt in the calpulli had their necks [ears?] pierced for bloodletting, and all the people drew their own blood; no one failed to do so, but all without exception shed blood and offered incense, and no one remained idle. And at that place stood the image, which was called the Eagle Vessel (Cuauhxicalli), where the image of the sun stood. It was painted in the manner of a human face with its rays of light going out from it in a circle, surrounded with great feathers, with red spoonbill feathers as its border, and before it was performed the drawing of blood, the offering of incense, the making of offerings, and the giving of various things. And on this feast day captives were put to death, and it was said that those who died in war went to dwell in the house of the sun, to live there beside the sun.

Account of the vows and oaths.

They used to make vows to the idols, to serve them, with some sacrifices and offerings, whenever one of their children, or someone of their household, fell ill, or suffered misfortune in their standing, or was injured. This they did not to one idol alone, but to two or three of their idols, so that they would help them in that need. They also had the custom of making oaths, to fulfill some matter to which one was bound; and the person to whom they were obligated would require that they make an oath, in order to be assured of their word. And the oath they made went in this form: "By the life of the sun, and of our lady the earth, I will not fail to do what I have said" — and for greater assurance, regarding the earth: then they would touch the ground with their fingers, bring them to their mouth, and lick them; and thus they would swear by the earth, making their oath. When, in some necessity, a person asked a god for help, he would make a vow and oath to do such a thing in his service, and would fulfill it.

[Nahuatl text, parallel account:] ...when the hearth is prepared, this is true.

Here is explained how prayers were made to the demons (the idols), and how oaths were made among them.

When an oath was to be made, if someone vowed his child to the demons — whether to one, or to two, or to three — whatever he promised to the demons, or if some misfortune befell his child, then a vow was made to the fire-priests. Likewise, an oath was made when someone accused another of something, so that it might be verified, it would be sworn. So that his word would be proven true, so that he would not be called a liar, he ate earth. Then at once the one who had been accused would eat earth, to confirm that his word was true, so that it would not be thought a lie; he would say that the sun and the Lord of the Earth well knew it, as he ate the earth. In this way the oath was made. And the prayers were performed only by means of the offering of incense, and gifts, together with the eating of earth, as a sign of confession.

There were also, in the temples, women who from early childhood were raised there: and the reason was that, out of devotion, their mothers, while they were very small girls, would promise them to the service of the temple; and at twenty or forty days of age they would present them to the one in charge of this, whom they called "quacuilli," who was like a priest: and they carried brooms to sweep,

Concerning the women of the temple, fo.145.

And an incense burner of clay, and incense called white copalli: all this they presented to the temple keeper or priest. Once this was done, the temple keeper charged the mother greatly to take much care in raising her daughter, and also that every twenty days she should take care to bring her to the calpulco or parish of her neighborhood, that same offering of brooms and copal and firewood to burn in the hearths of the church. That girl, once she reached the age of discretion, informed by her mother about the vow that had been made, would herself go to the temple where the other maidens were, carrying her offering with her, which was a clay incense burner and copal. From this time until she was of marriageable age, she always remained in the temple, under the charge of the matrons who raised the maidens.
